title: Variables
learningGoals: declare an `int` variable and assign a value to it
declare and initialise in one line
update a variable using its old value
always initialise before use and compile with `-Wall`

scenes.onScreen: A Mapusa fish market stall with labelled baskets: Bangda, Pomfret, Prawns
scenes.animation: Market ambience; baskets drop in; Xecxec peeks out of a basket
scenes.narration: Walk into Mapusa market on a Friday. Every basket has a label: bangda, pomfret, prawns. You never have to guess what's inside. That is exactly what a variable is in C. A labelled basket that holds a value.

scenes.onScreen: Last challenge answer; a row of memory boxes; one gets a label "age" and a value 19
scenes.animation: Label tag swings on with a clack; number drops in with a plop
scenes.narration: Last episode's challenge was to clean up an old program with a header comment, a few slash slash notes and four-space indents. If it still compiles and gives the same output, you nailed it. Now: your computer's memory is a long row of tiny boxes. A variable is one of those boxes, with a name stuck on it. We say, "Give me a box called age." C finds a free box, labels it age, and from then on, whenever we say age, C knows which box we mean. We can put a number in it, read it, or change it.

scenes.animation: Line highlights; memory box appears per declaration; variable tracker panel on the right
scenes.narration: Let's write it. [HL 5] Line five: int age, semicolon. This is a declaration. int means the box holds a whole number, an integer. age is the label. Right now the box exists, but we haven't put anything in it. [HL 6] Line six: age equals nineteen. This is an assignment. [TRACK age=19] The equals sign in C does not mean "is equal to". It means "put the value on the right into the box on the left". [HL 8] Line eight does both at once: int rollNo equals forty-two. [TRACK rollNo=42] This is called initialising: declare and give a starting value in one line. [HL 9] Line nine, same thing: int marks equals seventy-eight. [TRACK marks=78] Three baskets, three labels, three values.

code.output:
Age: 19
Roll no: 42
Marks after bonus: 83

scenes.onScreen: Lines 11–12, `%d` placeholder replaced by the value
scenes.animation: `%d` flips like a card to show 19; terminal strip shows output
scenes.narration: Now let's read a box. [HL 11] Line eleven: printf, "Age: percent d", comma, age. The percent d is a placeholder. It means "put a whole number here". After the closing quote, comma, age tells printf which number. So printf takes the value from the age box, nineteen, and puts it where percent d was. Output: Age: 19. [HL 12] Line twelve does the same with rollNo. Roll no: 42.

code.output:
Age: 19
Roll no: 42
Marks after bonus: 83

scenes.animation: Box value 78 lifts out, +5 joins, 83 drops back in; tracker updates
scenes.narration: The best part of a variable: it can vary. [HL 14] Line fourteen: marks equals marks plus five. In maths class, this line makes no sense. In C, read it right to left. First, take the value in marks, seventy-eight. Add five, eighty-three. Then put eighty-three back into marks. [TRACK marks=83] The old seventy-eight is gone. A box holds only one value at a time. [HL 15] Line fifteen prints it: Marks after bonus: 83.

code.output:

Roll no: 42
Marks after bonus: 83

scenes.onScreen: Naming rules: letters, digits, underscore; no digit first; no spaces; case matters; no keywords
scenes.animation: Bad names stamped with a red X; good names get a mint tick
scenes.narration: A few rules for names. Use letters, digits and underscore. A name cannot start with a digit, so 2ndMarks is not allowed. No spaces, so roll no is not allowed; write rollNo or roll_no. Capital letters matter: Age and age are two different boxes. And you cannot use C's own words, like int or return. Pick names that say what's inside, like we learned in episode six.
Why did the variable go to therapy? It had too many changes in its life.

scenes.onScreen: `int total;` used before assigning; garbage output; `-Wall` warning; fix
scenes.animation: Box shows "???" with dust; buzzer; then `= 0` drops in, success chime
scenes.narration: Today's bug prints a random number. Look: int total, semicolon. Then total equals total plus fifty. Then print total. You expect fifty. Run it. I got thirty-two thousand something. You might get zero, or a huge number, or something else. Why? When you declare a box without a value, C does not clean it. It holds whatever junk was left in that memory before. Junk plus fifty is still junk. GCC can warn you, but only if you ask. Compile with dash capital W, all. Now GCC says: warning, total is used uninitialized. From today, always compile with dash Wall. The fix: give total a starting value. int total equals zero. Now the output is Total: 50. Every time.

scenes.onScreen: Store age, height (in cm), roll number; print each on its own line
scenes.animation: Timer ticks; three empty boxes wait
scenes.narration: Your challenge. Create three variables: your age, your height in centimetres, and your roll number. Use whole numbers for all three. Print each one on its own line with a label. Compile with dash Wall, and make sure there are no warnings.
Next episode: data types. Why did two and a half kilos of fish become two kilos? Keep coding, says Xecxec!

bug.error:
**Without `-Wall`:** no message at all. **Wrong output** (a garbage value; on screen: "your number will differ"):

Total: 32815

**With `gcc -Wall`:**

bug07.c: In function 'main':
bug07.c:6:11: warning: 'total' is used uninitialized [-Wuninitialized]
    6 |     total = total + 50;
      |     ~~~~~~^~~~~~~~~~~~
bug07.c:5:9: note: 'total' was declared here
    5 |     int total;
      |         ^~~~~
bug.why: A local variable without a starting value holds leftover junk from memory, so always initialise it.

shorts.title: Variables are fish baskets
shorts.hook: "Every basket in the fish market has a label."
shorts.script: Every basket in the fish market has a label. You never guess what's inside. A variable in C is the same: a box in memory with a name on it. You can put a value in, read it, and change it. That's it. That's a variable.
shorts.caption: The easiest way to understand variables.

shorts.title: marks = marks + 5?!
shorts.hook: "This line breaks maths. But not C."
shorts.script: marks equals marks plus five. In maths, impossible. In C, read it right to left. Take the value in marks, seventy-eight. Add five. Put eighty-three back in the box. The equals sign in C means "store", not "is equal to".
shorts.caption: The equals sign is not what you think.

shorts.title: Why is my number random?
shorts.hook: "I added 50 to zero and got 32 thousand."
shorts.script: I added fifty and got thirty-two thousand. Why? I declared int total without a value. In C, that box holds leftover junk. Junk plus fifty is junk. Compile with dash Wall and GCC warns you: total is used uninitialized. Fix: int total equals zero.
shorts.caption: The bug that prints random numbers.

shorts.title: Variable therapy
shorts.hook: "Why did the variable go to therapy?"
shorts.script: Why did the variable go to therapy? It had too many changes in its life.
shorts.caption: It varies.

shorts.title: What does this print?
shorts.script: int x equals ten. x equals x plus x. x equals x plus one. Print x. What's the answer? ... Twenty-one. Ten plus ten is twenty, then plus one. Comment your answer before you check.
